articles.title: Nate Silver: GOP midterm sting ‘triggers the ending’ of Trump era
articles.summary: Polling analyst Nate Silver on Wednesday predicted that the Republican defeats in the 2026 midterm elections triggered “the ending” of President Trump’s era in U.S. politics. “Are you familiar with the term ‘denouement?’” Silver asked his “Still Counting” podcast co-hosts and former FiveThirtyEight colleagues Clare Malone and Galen Druke on their show. “You know, the…
articles.body:
Polling analyst Nate Silver on Wednesday predicted that the Republican defeats in the 2026 midterm elections triggered “the ending” of President Trump’s era in U.S. politics.

“Are you familiar with the term ‘denouement?'” Silver asked his “Still Counting” podcast co-hosts and former FiveThirtyEight colleagues Clare Malone and Galen Druke on their show. “You know, the key actions have kind of –– well, it depends, right? In a Shakespearean tragedy, then, you’d have things go totally mad over the next two years, right? So there’s that part of it.”

Silver, who predicted a potential “ blue tsunami ” that came to fruition on Election Day, called the results of the midterms “the climactic action that triggers the ending,” leaving it “hard to imagine” a point where Trump’s popularity rebounds before the end of his second term.

Malone compared the political moment to remarks made by political journalist Rachael Bade, who compared the Trump era to an “eight-book” saga beginning with Trump’s 2016 election victory and the seventh installment focused on the oncoming “clash between Trump and [a] Democratic Congress.”

Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress, with 55 seats in the Senate and 255 seats in the House, according to The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ. Republicans held on to 44 Senate seats and 168 seats in the House, while several races have yet to be called.

Trump and other administration officials have admitted that aspects of their policy decisions –– deportations and the Iran war , with the latter resulting in an increase in gas prices –– may have contributed to GOP losses.

But the outcome of the midterms and the lame-duck status of Trump’s second administration could open up discussions within the GOP about the future of the MAGA movement launched by Trump upon the start of his first presidential campaign in 2015.

About 45 percent of self-identified MAGA Republicans told Politico in a recent poll that their movement was a loser in the midterms. Fifty-nine percent of overall respondents said the same.

When asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper last month if an unsatisfactory midterm performance might signal the “beginning of the end for the MAGA movement,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) replied, “I do think there will be a debate in the party , and I think we need it.”

Some outlets have speculated on the future of Trump’s movement, though the president has said he believes it could still survive without him.

Members of his administration, like Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have been eyed as possible heirs to his legacy, particularly as both parties gear up for the next battle for the White House in 2028.

Trump said in an interview with “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat that he thinks the movement will go on without him.

“Because MAGA is basically common sense, you know?” he said. “MAGA’s strong borders, good military.”

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Heritage Foundation holds midterm postmortem and roast of John Thune
articles.summary: Heritage Foundation Forum attendees heard Chip Roy rail against filibuster excuses as conservatives debated how to recover from midterm losses.
articles.body: When the Heritage Foundation, a leading conservative think tank, started planning this week’s event, The Forum, at the Gaylord Resort at National Harbor in Maryland, organizers could not have known how catastrophic the midterm elections would be for Republicans. But as Kevin Roberts, the organization's president, told Fox News Digital, "I think it makes it even more important." The order of the day consisted of two basic questions: Why did the GOP get blown out last week, and how can the losses be recovered? When it came to the blame game, one name stood out: Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., was battered like a piñata and jeered by a crowd that looked too austere for jeering. From his opening remarks, Roberts accused Thune of engaging in "watered-down conservatism," and in my conversations with attendees, the rhetoric only got nastier. SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER "For decades now, we’ve had a Senate leadership whose game plan is losing slowly," Dan Schneider, vice president of the Media Research Center, told Fox News Digital, adding, "they see the bottom of Hell and just want to delay entrance into those chambers." Things didn’t get much better for Senate leadership when I spoke with Yoram Hazony, a leading intellectual in the national conservatism movement, who said, "People are so frustrated by the Save Act … If you had to pick one thing that just kind of broke everybody, it’s you’ve got this 80/20 issue, let’s get election integrity, there’s basically no Republican who doesn’t want it, so it just makes it inconceivable [that it wasn’t passed]." The SAVE America Act floundered because of Thune’s unwillingness to even hold a vote to bypass the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster threshold, an excuse that Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, told attendees he was frankly sick and tired of. "No more excuses. No more garbage about filibuster this, filibuster that," Roy railed from the podium. "I don’t want to hear any of the nonsense out of this town. I want delivery of freedom. I want delivery of limited government. I want delivery of security on our border, delivery of security on our streets, and I want everybody to shut the hell up if they’re not doing those things." At this point, with much steam having been blown off, everybody was ready for some lunch. As for how to reverse the losses suffered during the recent unpleasantness, some important points were made. Fox News contributor Ben Domenech said sensibly of courting the youth vote, "Stop making fun of guys in their basement playing video games, these are your voters." VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS Mary Katharine Ham, of the "Normally" podcast, urged attendees to understand that now, "every election is a vibes election, voters look for a party to punish. This time it was Republicans," which speaks to the lackluster performance of so many GOP candidates. One question I asked everyone I spoke with at the forum was whether the big midterm losses opened the door to a wider array of potential 2028 GOP presidential nominees than we thought we were looking at two weeks ago. Universally, the answer was yes. MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028 For months, even years, the names Vance, Rubio, Cruz and DeSantis have dominated the primary buzz. But on Wednesday, I heard names like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, New Hampshire Gov.-elect Kelly Ayotte, former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and even Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. As one older gentleman in attendance, a retired banker, told me, "When you get your ass kicked that badly you have to look far and wide to fix it." SENATE REPUBLICANS PLAN 54-DAY BLITZ TO PUSH TRUMP'S AGENDA BEFORE DEMOCRATS SEIZE POWER For his part, Kevin Roberts and the Heritage Foundation he leads are ready to work with all Republicans to get out of the political wilderness, even the much-maligned John Thune. "Heritage will of course work with anybody," Roberts told Fox News Digital. "President, vice president, leader Thune, even members of the other party if they want to focus on kitchen table issues," he said, adding that Republican senators need to "gum up some of the really radical legislation of the left." If the Heritage Foundation Forum is any indication — and let's face it, it is — then Thune has an enormous amount of work to do to win back the good faith of the conservative movement and Republican voters. A huge first step toward that would be to show some fire in his belly. With the loss of the House and Senate, the chance for Republicans to nuke the filibuster and make generational change in Washington has passed. Now, they can only hope that if Democrats win the presidency in 2028, they will show similar restraint. For now, in this period of political purgatory in which President Donald Trump will wait out his final two years in office, Thune needs to fight, albeit on defense, harder than he has ever fought. He has to show Republicans some spirit and no longer accept the leftward ratcheting of our governance. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP One can say that amid the midterm gloom, a funny thing did happen at the forum: a sense of hope, a feeling that Republicans have been here before and always get up off the canvas. Everyone I spoke with seemed ready for the fight.

articles.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded him at Arlington National Cemetery
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday awarded a commendation to the Army sentinel who reprimanded him and his guests for their behavior at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.
articles.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday awarded a commendation to the Army sentinel who reprimanded him and his guests for their behavior at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day. “We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth wrote in a post on X with a picture of him awarding Army Spc. Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for his action while guarding the site. Hegseth, his wife, Jennifer, and some of Hegseth’s top aides were taking pictures, talking and laughing in front of the tomb on Wednesday when Iglesias directed them to stop. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” he shouted. Hegseth did not acknowledge the reprimand at the time, and looked over his shoulder before continuing to walk up a set of stairs. Asked for comment after the incident, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth and the department “have always honored” service members’ sacrifices and praised Iglesias’ actions. “While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said in a statement. The medal Hegseth gave Iglesias is for service members who have “distinguished themselves by meritorious achievement or service,” according to the Army. Soldiers from the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, known as “The Old Guard,” stand watch at the tomb 24 hours a day, in part to make sure visitors behave respectfully. “In the early 1920s, people often used the Tomb as a picnic area. Today, challenges include tourists speaking too loudly or entering the post for a better picture,” according to the Pentagon’s website. The incident happened at a politically fraught time for Hegseth. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth earlier his week. The Republican-led House voted 211-204 to shelve the resolution, but Democrats are likely to renew efforts to oust him when they become the majority party in January. Hegseth blasted Massie’s effort as “political spectacle,” saying the impeachment push was “a farce and a stunt.”

articles.title: Inside Jim Jordan's effort to usher in new era of Republican leadership: 'He's a fighter'
articles.summary: Jim Jordan won the House GOP minority leader race over Steve Scalise by a 106-73 margin, and Republicans are rallying behind his combative style.
articles.body: Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, is set to take the reins of the House GOP in the next Congress, and his fellow Republicans are quickly rallying to tout him as the best person for the job. The current House Judiciary Committee chairman has enjoyed a high profile in the media for years, long known as a bomb-thrower ever since he helped found the conservative House Freedom Caucus in 2015. Because a House minority leader's primary job is to lead counter-messaging against the majority's agenda, Republican lawmakers are arguing Jordan is in a prime position to be throwing bombs at the other side — potentially weakening the Democratic majority's own argument to keep the House in 2028. "Right now, our goal is to stop bad ideas. And I think Jim will do a great job of articulating just how wild some of these ideas are," Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. LONGTIME GOP LEADER FACES UNCERTAIN FUTURE AFTER JIM JORDAN WINS HOUSE LEADERSHIP FIGHT Haridopolos is a longtime ally of House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., who notably lost this week's internal House GOP leadership election to Jordan by a 106 to 73 margin, sources told Fox News Digital. But even Scalise's supporters have quickly rallied behind Jordan since Tuesday's race. "Republicans took a hard hit last week, but now it’s time to come together and get back to work. I’m ready to help Jim and our team speak to every voter we need to win the majority back in 2028," Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, who told Fox News Digital he would vote for Scalise, posted on X after the election of Jordan. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald, R-Wis., a Jordan ally, noted the incoming minority leader has had experience sparring with Democrats on the Oversight and Judiciary committees, which will likely play a prime role in investigating — and potentially impeaching — members of the Trump administration. "That's going to wear thin in a hurry," Fitzgerald said of Democrats' plans. "[Jordan] understands it, because we've been on the other side of it." HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE In his six years as head Republican on the House Judiciary Committee, Jordan has cemented his reputation as a capable bulldog for President Donald Trump and the GOP. He's known for asking sharp, pointed questions of Democrat-leaning witnesses and spearheading investigations into justice officials who Republicans accuse of blocking Trump's agenda. "He definitely brings that athletic mentality to committee hearings. What you're gonna see in press conferences, you'll see it on the floor," said Russell Dye, a longtime former aide to Jordan. "You're gonna have a guy that's not just gonna lay down, he's going to get out there, attack, attack, attack, and do it in a way though, that normal Americans understand." "He's a fighter," Dye said. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who will be going into the next Congress as Jordan's No. 2, compared him to the "Energizer bunny" and praised him as a "decision-maker." And the Ohio Republican himself signaled that he sees his role as directing the voice of the opposition against a likely barrage of Democratic probes. MIKE JOHNSON NOT RUNNING TO LEAD HOUSE GOP AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSSES Jordan told "Hannity" on Wednesday night that Republicans would heavily focus their pushback during committee meetings, where those investigations and impeachment efforts traditionally start. "[Democrats are] just attacking their political opposition, but it'll be across the board in every single committee," Jordan said. "And we are committed, as House Republicans, to pushing back and giving the facts and the truth to the American people." But House Freedom Caucus Chairman Jordan and Minority Leader Jordan will be very different people, Republicans around him have said. The Ohio Republican has traded his days of publicly criticizing fellow GOP lawmakers in for public calls for unity, something sources said he stressed in his argument to win the leadership role last week. "He's evolved. He's been a mouthpiece for the party," Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., said. "He's intelligent. ... He's the right messenger for the right time, and he's been setting himself up for this for decades." But it remains to be seen if that pragmatism will extend to deal-making with Democrats. articles.title: Trump urges Senate leadership to move $350B reconciliation bill
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday renewed calls for the $350 billion military funding package to be passed through the Senate as time runs out for Republicans to hold a majority in Congress. “I rebuilt our Military in my First Term, and we’re doing it AGAIN, bigger and better than ever before! The Radical Democrat Majority in…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday renewed calls for the $350 billion military funding package to be passed through the Senate as time runs out for Republicans to hold a majority in Congress.

“I rebuilt our Military in my First Term, and we’re doing it AGAIN, bigger and better than ever before! The Radical Democrat Majority in the next Congress has already made it clear that their Number One Agenda is to BLOCK and RESIST this historic investment in our National Security,” Trump wrote Thursday on Truth Social .

“They want to leave our Warriors weak, and unguarded, but the American People want their Warriors SAFE and STRONG,” he continued. “That’s why TODAY I am calling on Senate Leadership to IMMEDIATELY move on the 350 Billion Dollar Reconciliation Bill to give our brave Warriors the DECISIVE ADVANTAGE they deserve.”

“Our Military must be strong, powerful, and respected. Republicans must deliver for our Warriors. The Democrats never will,” the president added. “The time is NOW.”

Republicans have only weeks to pass legislation before Democrats take the majority of both chambers come January after their big wins in the midterm elections last week.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has repeatedly pushed Congress to greenlight the reconciliation package — which includes several of Trump’s priorities — during speeches, events and on social media.

The Pentagon chief has argued the investment is critical for strengthening the military, expanding the defense industrial base and ensuring that the country’s national security is protected.

But several House Republicans last month warned that they were ready to block a partisan reconciliation package unless the administration gets tougher on Russia.

The package remains stalled in Congress over differences in how to pay for it, and some lawmakers have warned it is unlikely the $350 billion top line could be reached.

The $350 billion request includes $47 billion for expanded munitions production; $17 billion for the Golden Dome homeland defense system; more than $48 billion for critical minerals; and around $103 billion for low-cost autonomous systems, artificial intelligence and counter-unmanned systems.

articles.title: ‘Plenty of smoke’ around Trump administration corruption allegations: Ben Shapiro
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Ben Shapiro said Wednesday there is “plenty of smoke” around corruption allegations in the Trump administration. “Obviously, the fact that there’s so many people in the direct orbit of the president, who either have been taking advantage of his largesse, or who are directly related to people who are in the Trump family,…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Ben Shapiro said Wednesday there is “plenty of smoke” around corruption allegations in the Trump administration.

“Obviously, the fact that there’s so many people in the direct orbit of the president, who either have been taking advantage of his largesse, or who are directly related to people who are in the Trump family, that obviously has created massive blowback for the administration and for Republicans,” Shapiro said on NewsNation’s “On Balance.”

“And it’s very difficult to look at the reporting that’s been done and say that there is no fire at all here, because there certainly is plenty of smoke. And so, the sort of attempt by the administration to say that, ‘We’re taking on waste, fraud, abuse, corruption.’ That’s going to fall flat with the American people if they feel like everybody around you is getting rich and they are getting poorer.”

Shortly before this year’s midterms, in which Democrats took back the House and Senate, scandals affecting President Trump’s orbit were in the national spotlight .

Last month, reporting surfaced suggesting that then-U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle privately solicited cash to pay off debts prior to her confirmation hearing. And separate reporting came out that the president’s longtime campaign advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair went to the Balkans to advise a pro-Russian political party, with the two making hundreds of thousands of dollars in that effort.

Beyond the scandals involving Guilfoyle, LaCivita and Blair, ties that Trump and those in his orbit have to World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency firm Trump and his sons founded two years ago, have also come under scrutiny.

Financial disclosures showed Trump earned more than $500 million from the crypto venture, but the firm has said it has been set up in such a way that the Trump family can’t get involved in the bank when the president holds office.

articles.title: The top Trump officials Democrats admit are on their hit list for investigations in the new Congress
articles.summary: Democrats say Howard Lutnick, Stephen Miller, Tom Homan and Marco Rubio could face impeachment efforts and congressional hearings in January.
articles.body: Democrats are sharing their growing list of senior officials and advisors in President Donald Trump's administration who could face impeachment efforts and congressional investigations when they take control of Congress in January. Left-wing lawmakers are signaling that their oversight ambitions extend well beyond War Secretary Pete Hegseth after Tuesday's failed impeachment effort. Top House and Senate Democrats told Fox News Digital they are considering investigations, congressional hearings and potential impeachment proceedings targeting senior administration officials, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH "Our job of accountability doesn't change, we are going to hold everyone accountable that needs to be held accountable," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital when asked about possible action against Miller and Homan. "Especially if we've seen the violations and any kind of gross abuses." Gallego acknowledged that the details of any potential efforts to remove the officials "remain to be seen." Miller and Homan did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., who introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, echoed Gallego's remarks, signaling support for further accountability efforts in the House. HEGSETH COULD FACE NEW IMPEACHMENT PUSH OVER UKRAINE AID, LAWMAKERS WARN Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., also expressed support for increased congressional scrutiny, arguing that voters sent a message during the midterm elections. "What we heard from the American people on Tuesday (midterms) was to put an end to the corruption," Grijalva told Fox News Digital. "We're looking at the executive in the White House making hand over fist millions of dollars while in office," she continued. Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., the current vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus and a candidate to lead the conference in January, also backed discussions about potential investigations into Miller and Homan. Lieu told Fox News Digital that, if elected caucus chairman, he intends to discuss with Democratic leadership how to proceed with congressional hearings, investigations and possible impeachment proceedings targeting the two officials. The California Democrat also called for an investigation into Lutnick over allegations involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. NVIDIA SPY CASE EXPOSES HOW FOREIGN AGENTS TARGET AMERICA’S CORPORATE ELITE: 'HE IS COMPROMISED' "Howard Lutnick needs to be investigated over his role in Jensen Huang and the Chinese spy, we're going to have an investigation into those allegations, that's completely unacceptable," Lieu told Fox News Digital. Lieu alleged that Lutnick knew about the reported relationship but failed to investigate or take action. Lutnick did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a vice chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and member of the House Select Committee on China, also supported investigating Lutnick and did not rule out scrutinizing Rubio's potential involvement. DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY "I think we need transparency," Khanna told Fox News Digital. "I think we need to understand what they (Rubio and Lutnick) knew." "Rubio knew about the Chinese spy, and then got invited to the China trip," Khanna continued. "We need to get to the bottom of this." Rubio did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The lawmakers' remarks signal that Democrats could use their congressional majorities to expand oversight of Trump's administration, although no findings of wrongdoing involving the named officials have been established in the allegations presented. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While the House can impeach federal civil officers by a simple majority, conviction and removal require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Republicans, meanwhile, accused Democrats of pursuing politically motivated impeachment proceedings against Trump administration officials. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital following Tuesday's vote that he was "not surprised" by Democrats' interest in impeaching Hegseth. Mast argued that Democrats were determined to impeach "anyone who was appointed by the president," regardless of whether evidence supported the allegations.

articles.title: Trump says the U.S. doesn’t ‘need’ a deal with Iran
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said that the U.S. doesn’t need a deal with Iran despite repeatedly stating in the run-up to the midterm elections that one could be reached.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Thursday that the U.S. doesn’t need a deal with Iran despite repeatedly stating in the run-up to the midterm elections that one could be reached. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote in a Truth Social post, referring to the Strait of Hormuz. Trump said in the post that he asked Vice President JD Vance to focus not on diplomatic talks with Iran, but on alleged “crime and corruption” in “Democrat run Cities and States.” Days before the election, Vance had reached out to hard-liner Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in a bid to restart talks, The Wall Street Journal had reported. Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, had said a day after GOP losses in last week’s midterm elections that voter anger over the Iran war was the “real reason” for the party’s rout. It wasn’t immediately clear what prompted the president’s notable shift, as he had suggested numerous times before the election that the U.S. could reach an agreement to resolve the conflict with Iran in the near future. On the eve of the election, Trump wrote on Truth Social: “Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran. Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!” Trump’s post comes two days after he predicted at an impromptu White House news conference that the war is “going to be ending fairly soon.” He had met with the Qatari prime minister in the Oval Office Monday and wrote in a Truth Social post afterward that “Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History.” He added: “Should there be any change with respect to developments in the Middle East, the United States of America is ‘locked and loaded’ and ready to go. At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely. Israel, and the entire Middle East, are protected from Iranian danger and threats. We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected.” Hours later, Trump made a rare call into C-SPAN, and when asked how much longer the war with Iran could last, he said, “We could knock it out fast, or we could knock it out over a short, not a long period of time.” The president had said at the United Nations General Assembly in September that Iran was likely waiting to see the outcome of the midterm elections to make a deal. “I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.” NBC News reported last week that some of Trump’s advisers have told him that the window for restarting major combat operations in Iran was closing and that he should act before Democrats retake control of Congress in January, according to two U.S. officials. That timeline would require him to make a decision on Iran within weeks.

articles.title: Democrats turn on Schumer after historic election wins as potential challenger emerges
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer faces a fracturing caucus as Bernie Sanders, Elissa Slotkin and four newly elected senators reject his bid for Democratic leader.
articles.body: The calls for change that helped flip the Senate on Election Night have now reached the chamber itself, where some Democrats are turning their backs on Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer intends to seek another term as Democratic leader as his party prepares to take control of the Senate next year. But some of the progressive forces energized by the party’s blue-wave victories want to replace him, too. His caucus is fracturing over whether to support him, with longtime allies such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and newer members such as Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., having declared this week that they would not back him for leader. And Schumer’s detractors are eying Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has said that he’s "kicking the tires" on a 2028 presidential run, to challenge him. SCHUMER'S GRIP ON POWER SLIPS AS DEMS BEGIN TO REVOLT AGAINST HIM, EYE NEW LEADERSHIP Now he’s in listening mode and speaking with Senate Democrats about a bid against Schumer — and openly taking shots at the longtime Democratic leader, too, for siding "with the crypto industry" and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) against progressive candidates. "We just saw democracy in America in action. We should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate," Van Hollen said at the Popular Mandate conference this week. "We have two newly-elected senators who would not be there if Schumer and the DSCC had their way." When asked about a possible challenge from Van Hollen, Schumer said, "Chris Van Hollen and I are friends." "We talk frequently, and we're united, united in lowering costs and united in ending this damn war," he added, referring to the Iran conflict. BERNIE SANDERS DEMANDS DEMOCRATS BAN SUPER PACS FROM PRIMARIES, BLASTS AIPAC, ‘CORRUPT SYSTEM’ Outside the Senate in the adjacent office buildings, showings of support for Van Hollen took the form of blue, orange and pink sticky notes attached to a plaque outside his office. But for Schumer, a group of protesters chanted outside of his personal office "hey, hey, ho, ho, Chuck Schumer has got to go." Outside groups, like the progressive organization Indivisible, are bucking Schumer, too. They recently launched the "Tell Democrats: NO Schumer Coronation" campaign urging supporters to push their senator to not back Schumer. Schumer still has several allies in the caucus, including Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., who dismissed Van Hollen’s prospective challenge. SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS "Well, what's his record, other than yelling about anti-Israel stuff, or last year when he visited that wife beating guy in prison," Fetterman said, in reference to Van Hollen’s trip to visit Kilmar Abrego Garcia, his constituent who was mistakenly deported by the Trump administration. Several senators-elect that rode the blue wave to Washington, D.C., have publicly said they will not support Schumer for leader. Some were not the DSCC’s preferred nominees in key battleground primaries. Senators-elect Adam Hamilton, Peggy Flanagan, Scott Colom and Abdul El-Sayed have all publicly rejected Schumer as the Democratic leader. El-Sayed told Fox News Digital "time will tell" on how leadership elections will shake out, and whether Van Hollen has a strong enough coalition to beat Schumer. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think we'll see how things play out," he said. "This is a unique moment, and it's our job to make sure we honor our mandate." But Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirstin Gillibrand, D-N.Y., fiercely defended him on Tuesday. She lauded his "vision" for helping score several pick-ups in the cycle, and investing early in states like Mississippi. "And that is why you will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position," Gillibrand said. "We are about to win nine Senate seats. That has never happened in my political history."

articles.title: Jim Banks calls for Lutnick to testify on Nvidia CEO controversy, alleging ‘loophole’ use
articles.summary: Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify regarding his involvement with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, accusing Lutnick of using a “loophole.” “This news is as concerning as it gets,” Banks said Thursday during an appearance on Fox News. “When you’re in a war…
articles.body:
Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify regarding his involvement with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy , accusing Lutnick of using a “loophole.”

“This news is as concerning as it gets,” Banks said Thursday during an appearance on Fox News. “When you’re in a war with another country, you don’t give them your best technologies. And that’s why lawmakers, for the last two years, have been pushing hard to stop our high-end computer chips from being exported to China.”

The senator referenced his and Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s (D-Mass.) Guaranteeing Access and Innovation for National Artificial Intelligence (GAIN AI) Act, which would have required chipmakers to give U.S. firms first pick on advanced AI chips before selling to China or other countries of concern. Nvidia opposed the legislation in 2025, saying it would restrict competition, per Reuters.

“They [Nvidia] opposed other export control laws, and now we know that the Department of Commerce Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur,” Banks, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, continued. “Even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen.”

“So not only do I hope for Jensen Huang to come and testify, but I would like for Secretary Lutnick ASAP to come testify before the Senate Banking Committee,” the senator said.

He concluded that many Republican and Democratic senators on the committee had “questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year that would allow some of these issues to continue to occur.”

The Commerce Department is one of the major departments responsible for export controls — particularly AI chips sales to China. Lutnick was reportedly sent a classified memo concerning Huang’s affair and the potential security concerns, according to Axios .

The memo was first reported by The New York Times and was drafted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio to warn about Jensen Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

Three senior Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee are similarly demanding answers from Lutnick and asked him to halt exports of advanced AI chips.

“If Commerce was not briefed, we need to know why. If it was briefed, we need to know how it responded. And if the Department knowingly permitted these exports despite credible national-security concerns, the American people deserve an explanation,” they wrote in a letter sent Monday.

The Commerce Department did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Lawmakers want answers after Nvidia’s Huang steps down
articles.summary: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO amid an explosive spy scandal, but Washington isn’t letting him off the hook. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle said they still want to hear from the ex-Nvidia chief amid national security concerns about his involvement with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was passing information to China. “Jensen…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO amid an explosive spy scandal , but Washington isn’t letting him off the hook.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle said they still want to hear from the ex-Nvidia chief amid national security concerns about his involvement with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was passing information to China.

“Jensen and I have been very at odds, as some of you already know, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.) told reporters Thursday . “I don’t want to see anything hurt Nvidia.”

“But he has some very serious questions to answer,” he added.

Mast, who has long pushed for stricter chip export controls , said the former Nvidia CEO “agreed to come” in for a briefing that will likely be “under oath, transcribed, video recorded,” although negotiations are ongoing on the specifics.

Jensen Huang stepped down from his role leading the chipmaker on Thursday morning. It followed a bruising couple of days for the tech mogul and the company, which he founded in 1993 and turned into one of the most valuable firms in the world.

The former Nvidia chief admitted Sunday to having an affair with Alice Huang, a onetime executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed who is suspected of working as a Chinese intelligence asset.

The explosive revelations prompted bipartisan calls for an investigation into Jensen Huang and Nvidia, which don’t seem to be going away following his resignation.

Three top House GOP lawmakers — Mast; Rep. John Moolenaar (Mich.), chair of the House Select Committee on China; and Rep. Rick Crawford (Ark.), chair of the House Intelligence Committee — asked Jensen Huang last week to appear before Congress following initial reports of the affair.

Moolenaar said Thursday that his team is engaged in talks with Nvidia about having Jensen Huang testify. But the timing remains unclear, he added, not least because of the shake-up surrounding Jensen Huang’s resignation.

“I believe it’s important that we hear from him directly, as soon as possible,” the Michigan Republican said.

“I think it’s important that we have a deeper understanding of the national security concerns: How much information was gained by Chinese intelligence? The extent of their influence in terms of influencing policy discussions, and also chip diversion, either through smuggling or remote access,” Moolenaar added. “We want the entire picture.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) welcomed Jensen Huang’s resignation, but he said it’s not enough to allay concerns about the potential threat.

“It was the right thing to do,” he said Thursday during a press conference in the Capitol. “Now we have to get to the bottom of whether America’s national security has been compromised.”

Jeffries, who is poised to become Speaker in the new Congress come January, also amplified his earlier call for intelligence officials in the Trump administration to give a classified briefing to all members of Congress specifically on the Nvidia situation.

He said Democratic Reps. Jim Himes (Conn.), the incoming chair of the Intelligence Committee, and Gregory Meeks (N.Y.), who’s expected to lead the Foreign Affairs panel, will take the lead for House Democrats as they dig into the national security implications of the Jensen Huang scandals.

“We’ve seen the tip of the iceberg,” Meeks told reporters Thursday. “The board probably did what it had to do. I have other questions. This doesn’t make it go away.”

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) similarly told Fox Business that Jensen Huang’s resignation “does not absolve Nvidia from doing a full investigation of what happened” and “what sort of sensitive information may have been transmitted.”

“We need to do our own investigations as well from the Department of Justice,” he added.

As they prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats are also zeroing in on what the Trump administration knew and when.

President Trump was briefed about a year ago that the U.S. intelligence community believed Alice Huang was an operative for China’s government, The New York Times first reported last month. The president did not do anything with the information at the time, the Times reported, and even invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One when he flew to China in May.

But Trump said earlier this week he was told about the issue “not too long ago.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said Thursday that Congress “must demand answers” from Jensen Huang and others at Nvidia, while also arguing the Trump administration should answer for what it did after learning of Jensen Huang’s relationship.

“Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote in a post on the social platform X.

Other reports emerged this week that the Commerce Department last year paused its investigation into Megaspeed and whether it helped smuggle Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China despite U.S. export controls. Reports said Commerce passed the probe off to the Department of Justice (DOJ), though neither agency confirmed this. The DOJ declined to comment.

Axios also reported Wednesday that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled an authorization from Trump and other agency heads to crack down on firms suspected of diverting Nvidia’s chips to Congress.

“Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), a frequent critic of Jensen Huang, said Thursday.

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), who is seeking to become House Democratic Caucus Chair next year, pointed to these reports, telling The Hill, “I wish the administration had disclosed that to Congress and the American people.”

Other Democrats underscored Congress’s investigative role, saying they don’t have confidence in the Trump administration to take the lead given the president’s ties to Jensen Huang.

“Normally, I would say the Department of Justice should take a look at what happened there, [but] I don’t know that they’re up to the task right now. Certainly there’s a lane for congressional oversight,” Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.) said.

“We’ve got to get a better understanding of what happened there, and what the White House knew, and when they knew it, too,” Ivey added. “To the extent they knew some of that was going on but still let things move forward without disclosure, I think is disturbing.”

articles.title: Merkley to seek chairmanship of Environment and Public Works Committee
articles.summary: Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), a leading Senate progressive and strong advocate for the environment, says he will seek the chairmanship of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee. Merkley, is the ranking member of the Senate Budget Committee and would be in line to chair that committee in the next Congress, when Democrats will control…
articles.body:
Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), a leading Senate progressive and strong advocate for the environment, says he will seek the chairmanship of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

Merkley, is the ranking member of the Senate Budget Committee and would be in line to chair that committee in the next Congress, when Democrats will control at least 55 Senate seats next year.

“I am excited to announce the plan to seek the chairmanship of EPW in the next Congress,” Merkley said in a statement, referring to the Environment and Public Works Committee. “This committee has jurisdiction over a range of issues that are critical to American communities. Clean air and clean water matter to every American, no matter where they live.”

Merkley said he would prioritize “tackling toxics—ranging from asbestos to plastics to forever chemicals—that create significant health problems.”

He also said, “We need to strengthen our transportation infrastructure, which is essential to a thriving economy, and continue to address issues that sustain human health and our environment.”

The chairmanship of the Environment and Public Works Committee will be open because Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), who is the panel’s ranking member, is set to chair the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee next year.

articles.title: Pence leaves door open on 2028 presidential run
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence, who was President Trump’s second-in-command during his first term, is leaving the door open to a 2028 presidential bid. In a video interview with Fox News Digital published Thursday, Pence was asked if he was thinking about a presidential bid and a “timeline” on his decision, but he did not…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence, who was President Trump’s second-in-command during his first term, is leaving the door open to a 2028 presidential bid.

In a video interview with Fox News Digital published Thursday, Pence was asked if he was thinking about a presidential bid and a “timeline” on his decision, but he did not give a direct answer to either question.

“The truth is, if we don’t return the Republican Party to the principles of a strong defense, limited government, fiscal responsibility and the right to life, it won’t matter who we nominate in 2028,” Pence said in the interview.

“Because this version of Republicanism was just rejected by the American people,” he continued. “But, I have great hope; I was there the last time we lost the majority in 2006. I have great confidence in our new leadership in the Congress that they know the path forward. But, I can tell you that I don’t know what the future holds, but all of my energies, all of my focus and my calling, now, is to be a champion and an advocate for the conservative principles that have defined our party.”

Two months ago, Pence said he had “no plans” for a bid for the White House or any other elected office in 2028.

Economic Club of Washington, D.C., Chair David Rubenstein, during an event for the organization at the time, asked the former vice president if he would consider another go at the White House.

“What I can tell you is that we have no plans,” Pence responded.

Pence took on Trump in the 2024 GOP presidential primary. However, he later dropped out of the race following fundraising and polling trouble. Pence did not endorse Trump’s 2024 run and did not congratulate the president until after he won.

Trump and Pence’s relationship went south at the end of Trump’s first term, with Pence not stopping Congress’s certification of former President Biden’s victory in the 2020 election.

articles.title: Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday said he wants to “get Cuba done” before he leaves office and that the administration is “watching it very closely.” “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” he told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt. “We are watching it very closely, it’s doing very poorly,” the president said. “It’s essentially…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday said he wants to “get Cuba done” before he leaves office and that the administration is “watching it very closely.”

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” he told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt.

“We are watching it very closely, it’s doing very poorly,” the president said. “It’s essentially a failed, you know, place, nation, whatever you wanna call it.”

He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, “would love to do it.”

Trump also said he won the Cuban vote by a lot in Florida.

“I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” he continued.

When asked if he would be OK with the use of military force to free Cuba from its long-standing communist regime, the president said he “would certainly consider that.”

Trump has repeatedly suggested that an intervention of Cuba could be on the horizon. Earlier in the week, he said he thought Cuba “will fall fairly soon.”

“Cuba is falling. It’s a failing nation. It’s got an ideology very similar to what the Democrat ideology is, and it’s a failing nation. It’s a communist nation, socialist nation, sort of everything all wrapped in into one,” he said during a press briefing Monday, after a reporter asked if the president still planned on taking Cuba.

He added that the U.S. will help Cuba “on a humanitarian basis.”

During the United Nations General Assembly in September, Trump said the U.S. is seeking “fundamental change” from the island. And in March, the president said he believed he will have the “honor” of taking over Cuba.

“I think I can do anything I want with it,” he told reporters at the time. “Whether I free it, take it, I think I can do anything I want with it.”

The Trump administration announced another wave of sanctions against Cuba earlier this month that targeted 10 individuals and entities tied to the country’s government, military and oil industry.

The State Department, in its announcement, accused Cuba’s “ruling elite” of “hoarding the island’s energy, shipping, and technology resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, shortages, and a stagnant economy.”

Rubio last month said that Cuba has “already fallen” and is a “failed state.”

“It does not have a functional economy, and it is governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years,” Rubio told Fox News’s Sean Hannity. “It’s never worked.”

articles.title: Jeffries and Schumer have plenty of critics – but no challengers: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen explains why Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer don’t appear to be in much danger of losing their Democratic leadership bids.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen explains why Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer don’t appear to be in much danger of losing their Democratic leadership bids. Plus, Henry J. Gomez has an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at how Amy Acton overcame Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad in the Ohio governor’s race. — Adam Wollner Jeffries and Schumer have plenty of critics — but no challengers Analysis by Jonathan Allen Rep.-elect Bob Brooks, D-Pa., was one of a handful of so-called Bernie-Dog Democrats — endorsed by both democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and the House’s moderate Blue Dog Coalition — on the ballot this November. I traveled to his district in Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley in August as part of a reporting trip to eight swing districts across five states — a venture that revealed the disillusionment of MAGA voters and the anger of Democrats heading into the midterms before ballots were cast. At the polls, that anger was focused on voting Republicans out of Congress, and Brooks won by more than 12 points in a district that leaned marginally toward the GOP before. But some Democrats are also furious at their own party leadership for not being further to the left or not fighting hard enough against President Donald Trump. So, when I ran into Brooks at the foot of the Capitol steps during freshman orientation this week, I asked what he planned to do with his vote for speaker of the House. “There’s nobody else to vote for right now: It’s Hakeem Jeffries,” Brooks said of the New York Democrat who serves as minority leader and is so far running unopposed for the job. “I’m Team Hakeem right now.” An observer of social media feeds on the left could be forgiven for thinking that Jeffries is in danger of not becoming the first Black leader of either chamber of Congress in January. Some have argued that he has been “bought” by special interests. But interviews with lawmakers across the ideological and generational span of the Democratic caucus this week revealed no real schism over Jeffries. “It’s interesting because the outside conversations don’t match the internal conversations,” said Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-Conn. “No one else is putting their name in, and he delivered the largest majority.” It’s that last point that matters most for Jeffries, as well as for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is facing even louder rumblings about his bid for majority leader. For all of the consternation among activists over the last two years about the failure of Democrats in Congress to take on the president effectively, it was Trump who lost touch with the American public — in part because Democratic leaders didn’t shoot their party in the foot. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is gauging his colleagues’ support for a challenge to Schumer. Sanders and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., have said publicly that they don’t support Schumer’s bid. But the ambitions of Van Hollen and Slotkin, both of whom are often mentioned as potential 2028 presidential candidates — and Sanders’ tireless efforts to push the Democrats to the left — should not be confused with widespread disapproval of Schumer inside his caucus, even as several of the incoming freshman senators are opposed to him or noncommittal. He is on track to win a secret ballot for majority leader after Thanksgiving. If either Schumer or Jeffries were truly vulnerable, there would be plenty of candidates climbing all over one another to run against them. So far, there are none. How Amy Acton overcame big money and a vicious attack ad to make history in Ohio By Henry J. Gomez Amy Acton’s running mate saw the ad first. Shortly after 8:30 p.m. on a Monday night in mid-October, David Pepper was entertaining local Democrats over dinner at the Old Canal Smoke House in Chillicothe, Ohio, when he peeked at his phone. There in Pepper’s X feed was Acton’s long-estranged mother, in a 60-second video, calling her daughter a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her to be the state’s next governor. To Acton and her advisers, the possibility that Republican Vivek Ramaswamy would enlist the help of Donna Arthur — a woman she had not seen or spoken to since her stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child — was revolting. But it was a scenario they had braced for, based on Arthur’s previous public criticism of Acton and on their low opinion of Ramaswamy’s principles. Fifteen days before Election Day, it had arrived. Pepper, an experienced political hand who had chaired the state party and was now running for lieutenant governor, copied a link to the video in a text message to Acton and hit send. The news quickly reached the key members of Acton’s team and upended their evenings. That night, a plan months in the making was activated. They already had Acton’s brother on camera recalling the abuse they had endured as children, footage that would be harvested to produce an immediate response ad. In the morning, police and court records that documented the rape case against Acton’s stepfather — which had long ago been obtained by the campaign’s researchers — would be shared with reporters and circulated online. “We didn’t sleep a ton that night,” senior adviser Justin Barasky said. “It was one of those things that’s like, ‘Oh, God, these next few days are going to be brutal.’ But I think we seized on it.” Two weeks later, Acton made history as the first woman elected as Ohio’s governor — and the first Democrat to get the job in 20 years. This account of how she prevailed is based on interviews with more than a half-dozen people who worked on or closely with the Acton campaign, as well as others with firsthand knowledge of developments that shaped the race. Keep reading Henry’s exclusive report → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Mamdani prepares to fulfill promise to axe NYPD unit responsible for controlling protest violence
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani is reportedly preparing to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group after months of failing to fulfill his promise to do so.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is reportedly preparing to announce his plan to disband the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG), fulfilling a long-held campaign promise that has led to mounting pressure from his base, as well as questions about how the group's duties will be replaced. Politico reported that Mamdani, a democratic socialist, is preparing to announce plans to disband the unit, which responds to protests, civil disturbances and major events while handling counterterrorism operations. Mamdani has said he wants to decouple the unit’s protest and counterterrorism functions, but at a March City Council budget hearing Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said discussions with the mayor concerned "the future of how we police protests generally," not disbanding the unit. MAMDANI IN HOT SEAT OVER POST MOURNING DEATH OF INMATE CHARGED WITH CALLOUS CRIME: 'ABSOLUTELTY SHAMEFUL' The NYPD says the SRG responds to citywide mobilizations, civil disorders and major events and is a "critical asset" during parades, protests and the papal visit. SRG personnel are "also deployed to areas requiring an increased police presence due to increased crime or other conditions" and "mobilizes for shootings, bank robberies, missing persons, demonstrations, or other significant incidents," according to the department. Tisch added during the March City Council budget hearing that the SRG does not typically deal with peaceful protests, but is deployed for protests that involve criminal activity. She also noted that in 2025 the NYPD facilitated 4,255 protests and the SRG was available at 245 of them, or roughly 6%. Sources familiar with the plan told Politico that City Hall has been contemplating putting the SRG under Mamdani's new Office of Community Safety, launched earlier this year. The sources also said Mamdani's plan could be formalized via an executive order, according to Politico. MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS "I've been clear that my vision is for the disbanding of the SRG. And the reason for that vision is that the SRG were created a little more than a decade ago with an intention first of dealing with threats, terroristic threats to the city," Mamdani said during a press conference in September. "What it has eventually become is both dealing with counterterrorism and responses to exercising First Amendment rights," the mayor continued. "I do not believe that those purposes need to be dual purposes. I believe that we should have a focus on counterterrorism that is separate from our response to the use of First Amendment — [that] continues to be a conversation I'm having with our police commissioner." articles.title: LGBTQ representation on TV fell during 2025-26 season, GLAAD says
articles.summary: LGBTQ representation on TV fell during the last year, according to a new study by advocacy group GLAAD. The annual “Where We Are on TV” report found LGBTQ characters in scripted-series shows decreased by 25 percent from the previous season, dropping from 489 characters to 369. Researchers noted the difference was driven by a drop…
articles.body:
LGBTQ representation on TV fell during the last year, according to a new study by advocacy group GLAAD.

The annual “ Where We Are on TV ” report found LGBTQ characters in scripted-series shows decreased by 25 percent from the previous season, dropping from 489 characters to 369. Researchers noted the difference was driven by a drop in transgender characters, which fell 79 percent.

Queer characters were the next demographic to fall, with representation declining 50 percent. Representation of gay characters fell 32 percent, lesbian characters fell 14 percent and bisexual characters fell 5 percent. The only demographic that rose was nonbinary characters, whose representation increased by 33 percent.

The totals for LGBTQ characters on broadcast and cable TV also marked a 12- and 16-year low, respectively.

“In the last couple years, trans people have been scapegoated by the media. They have been targeted in ways that are offensive and dangerous. Lives have been lost,” Raina Deerwater, associate director of entertainment research and analysis for the GLAAD Media Institute, said in a statement. “Often we see media reflecting that, and because of a lot of the political conversation, it’s not a surprise to see trans representation falling on TV.”

Since President Trump entered the White House for a second time, legislation targeting transgender athletes has been on the rise. Red strongholds were quick to pass bans on transgender women and girls from female sports teams .

Deerwater called the trend “very disheartening,” adding that projects from transgender artists “aren’t being greenlit, so they have to tell them outside of traditional venues.”

Though TV production fell since the last season, GLAAD mentioned in its analysis that LGBTQ representation doubly outpaced this, saying it “does not account for the size of the drop in LGBTQ representation.”

articles.title: Petition to make Ayanna Pressley next Speaker garners more than 58K signatures
articles.summary: A Change.org petition requesting Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) be named the next Speaker of the House has received more than 58,000 signatures as of Thursday evening. The petition, released last Friday, was set up by the Coalition for Speaker Ayanna Pressley, “progressive activists from across the country dedicated to electing” the lawmaker to lead her…
articles.body:
A Change.org petition requesting Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) be named the next Speaker of the House has received more than 58,000 signatures as of Thursday evening.

The petition, released last Friday, was set up by the Coalition for Speaker Ayanna Pressley, “progressive activists from across the country dedicated to electing” the lawmaker to lead her party in the House.

It has received 58,503 signatures as of 5 p.m. EST on Thursday.

The coalition said in a statement that Pressley “represents a beacon of hope and integrity in a tumultuous political landscape.” It praised her record and leadership on issues like criminal justice reform and climate change, adding that electing her was “not just about politics.”

“Her ability to foster meaningful conversations and build bridges across the political aisle makes her uniquely qualified for this pivotal role,” the group said. “In a divided Congress, her role as a fair and balanced leader will be crucial in driving [bipartisan] legislation that addresses the needs of all Americans.”

The group added that Pressley’s leadership style “aligns with what the majority of Americans want to see in their government,” and that she “listens to her constituents … making informed decisions that reflect the diversity and complexity of our society.”

Common Dreams first reported on the petition Wednesday.

Pressley has not expressed interest in launching a bid to challenge the Speakership from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to become the country’s first Black Speaker at the start of the 120th Congress in January.

She did, though, call on Democrats to meet the expectations from voters after the party made sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections last week, calling on her colleagues to be “the FIGHTERS in the room,” according to a social media post Tuesday.

The petition comes as some progressive Democrats question Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) leadership ahead of the party’s dominance in both chambers of Congress.

Schumer faces a rebellion of his own, with some Senate Democrats and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who caucuses with Democrats, saying they will not back the New York Democrat as Senate majority leader. Sanders said the moment calls for greater action in responding to issues like the cost of living and wealth inequality.

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction? No,” he told reporters

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has been seen as a potential challenger to Schumer. He said Monday that he was in “ listening mode ” as he considers running for the role.

articles.title: Shaheen, Tillis demand probe into Ukraine Starshield restrictions
articles.summary: Outgoing bipartisan senators outraged over Ukrainian reports of interruptions to military-grade satellite access are calling for Congress to pursue accountability for the shutdown, focusing on Elon Musk’s company SpaceX and the Pentagon. Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) issued a statement obtained exclusively by The Hill urging Congress to conduct oversight on Kyiv’s…
articles.body:
Outgoing bipartisan senators outraged over Ukrainian reports of interruptions to military-grade satellite access are calling for Congress to pursue accountability for the shutdown, focusing on Elon Musk’s company SpaceX and the Pentagon.

Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) issued a statement obtained exclusively by The Hill urging Congress to conduct oversight on Kyiv’s reports of disruptions to Starshield satellites, impacting the country’s ability to defend against Russian attacks.

“Congress must determine who ordered or approved these disruptions and hold those responsible accountable,” the senators, who are both leaving at the end of the 119th Congress, wrote in a statement.

“The Pentagon and SpaceX must preserve all records, turn over the contracts and communications Congress needs to establish the facts, and put safeguards in place so this never happens again.”

The lawmakers called it “outrageous” that Ukraine was reporting disruptions to Starshield for the second time in about four weeks. Ukraine uses Starshield systems to direct drones and munitions for offensive and defensive capabilities. Starshield services stopped working for objects traveling more than 100 mph, Ukraine’s top diplomat in the U.S., Denys Sienik, said in a statement Thursday.

“We experienced speed limitation as of now on Ukrainian occupied territories and across the contact line,” said Sienik, who serves as deputy chief of mission and chargé d’affaires at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

“The contact line is the first line of our defense and the first point for interception of Russian drones,” Sienik said, noting the slowdown started gradually several days ago. “We don’t have clarification from SpaceX or Pentagon at the moment.”

Last month, Musk publicly acknowledged slowing down Starlink satellite systems over Ukraine for what he said was Kyiv’s violation of terms of service, using the systems for offensive actions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also downplayed Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military-grade satellite system contracted with the Pentagon. He said Ukraine was obligated to abide by the commercial terms of service for Starlink.

“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio told reporters last month .

Shaheen and Tillis urged their colleagues to keep pressure on the Trump administration and SpaceX to give Ukraine the tools to defend itself in the face of severe and ongoing Russian bombardment.

“Ukraine’s military has determined that these disruptions are systematic restrictions, and SpaceX admitted last month that it limited Ukraine’s service,” they wrote.

“SpaceX has yet to offer any explanation for these latest disruptions. These repeated restrictions raise further dire questions about why Ukraine is being deliberately deprived of the capabilities it needs to defend itself.”

Russia bombarded Ukraine overnight Tuesday into Wednesday with 163 drones, including 91 jet-powered drones flying upward of 310 mph, loitering munitions and at least one cruise missile, according to an analysis by the Institute for the Study of War.

At least six Ukrainian large power substations were hit by the Russian strikes. Power transmission lines and a heating facility were also struck, and power outages occurred in at least eight administrative regions.

The Starshield slowdown also comes as Ukrainian and Russian delegations wrapped up two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks in nine months, and that resulted in an agreement on a large swap of prisoners of war .

Shaheen and Tillis said Ukraine is negotiating in good faith while Russia continues attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure.

“Russia has shown no such good faith,” they wrote.

“While President Trump’s envoys travel to Moscow, [Russian President Vladimir] Putin continues attacking innocent civilians, including bombing a center in Kremenchuk serving children with special needs. Just last week, Putin killed 55 civilians as they were attempting to get humanitarian aid.”

articles.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher defeats Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas governor’s race
articles.summary: Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projected Thursday, extending the party’s hold on the office in the red state.
articles.body: Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projected Thursday, extending the party’s hold on the office in the red state. Holscher defeated Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, to succeed two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. While Trump carried Kansas — a state where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1 — by double digits in the latest three presidential elections, polling had shown a close race down the stretch due mostly to voter frustrations with Trump and his handling of the economy. Democrats also benefited from increased attention on the traditionally conservative state as its Senate race tightened. Holscher’s victory came despite a nearly 3-to-1 Republican ad spending advantage in the general election, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact. In the general election, Holscher aggressively tied Masterson to Trump, while also maintaining that she’d find areas to work with the administration. “I think that’s a concern that [Masterson] has the ear of the administration, because the administration also has a hold on him. You won’t see Ty Masterson pushing back against bad policy, like tariffs that are hurting our farmers or the importing of beef that are hurting our ranchers,” she told local news station KMBC in October. She added that will also “work with folks” in the administration “to make sure we bring good things to Kansas.” Masterson, who was endorsed by Trump, attempted to distance himself from the president on his website and in campaign materials. But his connection to Trump, who faced increasingly lower approval ratings in the traditionally red state, was unmistakable: the president came to Kansas over the last weekend before Election Day to campaign alongside Masterson and the Republican candidate in the state’s Senate race, Sen. Roger Marshall, who lost his re-election bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton. Meanwhile, Holscher also prominently highlighted her opposition to new data center construction throughout her campaign. “This field of Kansas sunflowers is under threat because big tech wants to build a day out of center. As governor, I’ll hit pause on data centers until we can set up firm guardrails to protect our communities and our budgets,” she said in one spot featuring her standing in a field. Masterson has opposed a moratorium on data centers and has defended a 2025 law he voted for giving a sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher has called for a statewide moratorium on the new data center construction. Building the Future, a pro-data center super PAC, jumped into the race last month to boost Masterson. Holscher’s win followed a primary that featured Democratic infighting. Kelly, who has maintained strong job approval ratings in the state, had endorsed Holscher’s Democratic primary opponent, state Sen. Ethan Corson, and issued stark warnings to voters about being “very concerned about the direction Kansas will go in” if Holscher were to win. Holscher had run a more progressive-styled campaign, while Corson ran as a moderate. Kelly endorsed Holscher following the primary.
