articles.title: 5 takeaways from Nvidia’s Jensen Huang scandal
articles.summary: Corporate America is in the midst of its most dramatic scandal in years. Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of Nvidia, resigned Thursday after admitting to one extramarital affair, with a woman suspected of being a Chinese agent, and amid new reporting of a second affair, this time with an Nvidia colleague. The vast company…
articles.body:
Corporate America is in the midst of its most dramatic scandal in years.

Jensen Huang, the CEO and co-founder of Nvidia, resigned Thursday after admitting to one extramarital affair, with a woman suspected of being a Chinese agent, and amid new reporting of a second affair, this time with an Nvidia colleague.

The vast company is at the epicenter of the artificial intelligence boom, primarily through its high-powered chips and the software that supports them. It also plays an increasingly important role in financing other elements of the AI build-out.

Jensen Huang’s fall is an astonishing denouement after a rise that saw him build Nvidia into a tech behemoth that, at its peak in October, was closing in on a $6 trillion valuation and was the world’s most valuable company. Apple has now reclaimed that crown.

Jensen Huang’s fall, and the circumstances surrounding it, also raise many political questions. Here are five takeaways.

Mystery remains around alleged Chinese spy

The core of the scandal is Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, to which he has admitted.

Any prominent CEO of an American company having an illicit relationship with a suspected Chinese agent would be an obvious problem. But that’s especially so given the centrality of AI to the American economy — and to national security.

Last year, a senior adviser for technology analysis at RAND, Jimmy Goodrich, wrote that high-performance computing systems form “the bedrock of American defense innovation.”

But the issue with the Alice Huang affair is more specific.

The U.S. has been restricting the sale of top-grade chip technology to China since 2022. In 2023, Alice Huang took control of Megaspeed, a company based in Singapore. In summary, Megaspeed became a major Nvidia customer — and is now suspected of funneling its products to China, in defiance of export controls.

Alice Huang does not appear to have made any public comment about the allegations. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and said in a Thursday statement, as reported by NBC News , that it had cooperated with previous inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce and “stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”

The Chinese government is characterizing the whole episode as a false smear campaign.

But in the U.S., the concern — as yet unproven — is whether the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang involved any underhanded business actions or covert understandings.

There are also obvious questions about Jensen Huang’s honesty with Nvidia’s board, and whether any corporate communications from the company were misleading.

President Trump has often evinced enthusiasm for what Jensen Huang has accomplished at Nvidia.

His admiration appears to have been rooted in at least two factors: his belief that the company was keeping the U.S. in the lead in the AI “arms race,” and a keen appreciation of the eye-popping profits Nvidia is making.

Trump also appeared fairly unperturbed by the scandal when it first became public. On Sunday, he called Jensen Huang “ an honorable guy ” who had done “an amazing job for our country.”

Even after Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, Trump wrote on social media that the former Nvidia chief had done “a fantastic job” — and suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook as his replacement.

But there are more specific issues that Trump has not addressed in any depth.

As a New York Times timeline of the matter outlines, Trump was reportedly told in October 2025 that Jensen Huang was close to Alice Huang — they are, of course, not related — and that U.S. intelligence suspected she was a Chinese asset.

But Trump does not appear to have taken any action on that information— and, the Times noted, cleared a higher-grade of chip for export to China two months later.

In May of this year, Jensen Huang was among the U.S. CEOs who accompanied Trump on his trip to China, where the commander in chief met with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

As that trip was getting underway, Trump took umbrage at press reports that Jensen Huang had not been invited. “In actuality, Jensen is currently on Air Force One,” Trump wrote on social media at the time.

An approach that perhaps looked supportive of an American business titan in May will look reckless to some eyes now.

The scandal has sparked tensions in Trump’s Cabinet

The mushrooming scandal has reportedly caused tensions among other high-profile members of the Trump administration.

Axios on Wednesday reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had “confronted” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the failure of Lutnick’s department to put Megaspeed on a de facto blacklist.

The Commerce Department’s entities list names companies and individuals that are believed to pose national security concerns to the U.S. While the list does not mean a blanket sanction is applied, it does generally require stricter export controls.

The backdrop here is the Trump administration’s perceived reluctance to add names to the list for fear of exacerbating tensions with China.

A Commerce Department spokesperson denied to Axios that such a clash took place, but a similar face-off was later independently reported by The New York Times .

There was never a good time for the Huang scandal to surface, but its emergence now coincides with broader nervousness about the durability of the AI boom.

Those concerns have multiple facets. Two of the main ones are doubts about whether the promised productivity gains from AI will be realized, and what happens to sky-high market valuations once the pace of infrastructural build-out begins to slow.

Nvidia shares had begun to slip before the current scandal came to light.

Tech shares in general also fell sharply two days after the midterm elections, a decline partly sparked by fears that newly empowered Democrats would be more inclined to regulate the industry and more reluctant to approve the construction of new data centers.

On Thursday, Nvidia shares declined by roughly 4.3 percent — a sharp fall, though not as catastrophic as some had feared. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index only experienced a very modest loss of less than half of one percent.

That said, any prolonged weakness for Nvidia, especially as it searches for a new CEO, could ripple through the AI ecosystem.

Months before the current saga erupted, some voices were being raised in concern about the massive corporation’s willingness to help finance other companies’ AI-related enterprises. Defenders of this approach say it keeps the foot on the accelerator of AI development. Critics worry that it’s a form of “circular investing” that leaves the whole industry vulnerable to a major bursting of its collective bubble.

It matters, even if you don’t own AI stocks

The saga isn’t only important for AI investors.

AI has become vital to American economic growth. On Wednesday, Goldman Sachs forecast that AI-related spending could amount to almost 4 percent of the entire U.S economy by the end of next year.

Of course, the Huang scandal doesn’t undo that in an instant. Optimists argue bullishness about AI is fully justified and will rampage onwards.

Still, Nvidia has lost almost one-third of its total value since its October peak.

That’s a serious drag on an industry that skeptics worry has become priced for perfection.

articles.title: Senate Democrats weigh December funding deadline to force an end to Iran war
articles.summary: Some Senate Democrats are looking to use a looming government funding deadline to force the Trump administration to end the war in Iran. While party leaders have yet to decide on whether to risk a shutdown, the desire for action from a mix of progressives and moderates could throw a wrench into the end-of-year legislative…
articles.body:
Some Senate Democrats are looking to use a looming government funding deadline to force the Trump administration to end the war in Iran.

While party leaders have yet to decide on whether to risk a shutdown, the desire for action from a mix of progressives and moderates could throw a wrench into the end-of-year legislative crunch.

Government funding is set to run out on Dec. 11 without action from Congress. Democrats and Republicans almost unanimously approved a short-term funding patch on Sept. 1, delaying the fight until after the midterm elections.

But after a sweeping victory, Democrats have the wind at their backs and are looking to use that momentum to bring an end to the Iran war, which members of both parties say is something voters want.

Some members say they should use the funding deadline as leverage.

Sens. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) said in a joint statement Thursday that they will oppose any short-term spending patch that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“As we approach the December 11 funding deadline, we should not accept a short-term spending deal that continues to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice,” the senators said.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) told reporters Thursday he also would not support any short-term continuing resolution (CR) unless it blocks money for the war.

Kaine said he is crafting a provision to block the administration from spending money on the Iran war that could be added to the next short-term spending bill. Kaine said he is working on it “in tandem with others,” but he did not specify whom.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” Kaine said when asked about priorities in short-term patch negotiations. “I mean, I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I told everybody that’s what I’m doing.”

But it remains uncertain how widespread that sentiment is among the caucus in the Senate, where any short-term bill would need about seven Democratic votes.

Sen. Patty Murray (Wash.), the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, said Democrats are discussing options for how, or even whether, to use the Dec. 11 deadline as leverage.

“We’re going to look at every tool we have available,” Murray said Tuesday when asked about restricting the war.

Murray also said she wants a short CR that would keep the government open until next year and allow Democrats to hammer out their long-term spending priorities when they take control.

Several Democratic senators were noncommittal when asked Thursday if they would hold up funding without an end to the war.

“I hope that’s not going to happen,” Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) said when asked if she would be willing to shut down the government over a war-related stalemate. “I hope that reasonable minds will realize that we have to stop the bleeding by stopping the war.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said Thursday that “there should be probably a short-term CR” to fund the government and that “there needs to be some action to end the war.” But he did not commit to whether his vote on the former was based on the latter.

“I’m not drawing lines in the sand right now,” Blumenthal said. “I’m telling you what the goal, my goal, is.”

Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) also said she wants to achieve both goals without specifying if they must be done together.

“We’re going to do everything we can to bring an end to this illegal war and to keep the government open and funded,” Baldwin told reporters Thursday when asked if she would prefer a CR without war language.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) would not say Thursday if he would withhold short-term funding over Iran war demands, deferring to the leaders on the appropriations committees — but Democratic votes may not be needed for a CR in the House.

“With respect to the appropriations process, right now there are four corners negotiations that are ongoing led by [Rep.] Rosa DeLauro [D-Conn.]… and she’s working through all of our Democratic priorities to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11,” Jeffries said at a press conference Thursday. “I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine, to [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East.”

Trump and Republicans could also throw the negotiations into chaos.

Republicans are weighing using their final weeks in power to cram through billions in defense spending, potentially as part of a party-line reconciliation package. Trump called Thursday for Congress to move fast on it.

Doing so would almost certainly further rile up Democrats.

“Any kind of tricks or gimmicks certainly threaten potential agreements,” Blumenthal said, when asked separately Thursday if Republicans using reconciliation would harm the short-term negotiating process.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), the likely next Democratic whip, did not want to speculate when asked if Congress was risking a shutdown by threatening war funding.

articles.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher wins Kansas governor's race, extending party's hold on governor's mansion
articles.summary: Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher wins the Kansas governor's race over Trump-backed Republican Ty Masterson, keeping the governor's mansion in Democratic hands.
articles.body: Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher won the Kansas governor’s race, defeating Republican Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson in the open contest to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, The Associated Press projected.The victory keeps the governor’s mansion in Democratic hands and marks the third consecutive Kansas gubernatorial election won by a Democrat. Kelly won the office in 2018 and secured a second term in 2022. The result underscores Democrats’ continued success in Kansas gubernatorial races despite Republicans’ longstanding dominance in the state’s presidential elections. The GOP has carried Kansas in every presidential election since 1968. GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS Holscher has served in the Kansas Senate since 2021 after previously spending four years in the state House. She secured the Democratic nomination after defeating fellow state Sen. Ethan Corson, who was endorsed by Kelly and former Democratic Gov. Kathleen Sebelius, in the August primary.Holscher faced scrutiny during the campaign over resurfaced social media posts from 2023 in which she suggested Jesus Christ could have been transgender. The comments came during a debate over proposed Kansas legislation restricting drag performances in front of children. Holscher celebrated her victory in a post on X, thanking Kansas voters as she prepared to take office. THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS "Thank you, Kansas! It’s the honor of a lifetime to serve as your next Governor," Holscher wrote. Masterson, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump in the crowded GOP primary, conceded the race in a post on X and said he had called Holscher to congratulate her. articles.title: DOJ has no ‘investigations into words’ of Democrats, Todd Blanche says
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche says there are no investigations into words of Democrats
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday there were no criminal investigations by the Justice Department into words spoken by senators or members of Congress, the same day that President Donald Trump once again called for six Democrats to be prosecuted over a social media video they posted last year. “There’s no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said,” Blanche said at a news conference at the Justice Department. Blanche’s comments came hours after Trump called for six sitting members of Congress to be charged over their speech in a social media video in which they told members of the intelligence and military communities not to obey unlawful orders. The Trump administration attempted to indict the the lawmakers earlier this year, but a federal grand jury in Washington unanimously rejected the charges. “Will the Seditious Six ever be prosecuted? What they did was a great violation to our Country and its Constitution!” Trump posted on his social media website on Thursday morning. Earlier in the week, the White House warned congressional Democrats that efforts to investigate the administration could be a crime. And on Wednesday, a top federal prosecutor sent a letter to a senator suggesting the lawmaker was under a civil rights investigation for his congressional probe of donors to Trump’s White House ballroom. Blanche said he believed Americans should be worried by the rhetoric coming from some politicians since Democrats won the majority in both the House and Senate during the midterm election last week. “Free speech is allowed,” Blanche said on Thursday. “But there can come a point when a criticism becomes a threat, and then when a threat becomes something criminal.” Blanche said that point hadn’t been reached. The U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, who was recently named a top federal prosecutor after losing his race for attorney general, sent a letter this week demanding Sen. Richard Blumenthal preserve records in connection with a congressional investigation into donors to the White House ballroom project. Reitz, a former chief of staff to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, alleged it was harassment of citizens. In response to the letter, Blumenthal said in a statement that he would not be intimidated and that he’d continue his investigation into the ballroom. On Thursday, Blanche said Reitz was a “great U.S. attorney,” but did not explain why a prosecutor in Texas would be investigating a lawmaker in Washington, D.C., who is from Connecticut, nor did he explicitly state if Reitz had his approval before publicly announcing the inquiry on social media. “Any office could investigate that,” Blanche said, when asked about the Reitz letter. “I’m the attorney general, so I don’t oversee every single thing that’s done, but yes, DOJ leadership is working with every U.S. attorney, including U.S. Attorney Reitz, on ongoing investigations.” Trump last week ordered the Justice Department to investigate Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, claiming her remarks at a school amounted to a “criminal act.” In her remarks, Slotkin sent a “deterrence message” to those thinking about joining the Trump administration. “The Department should stop threatening our constitutional freedoms and make clear that you will not again launch another frivolous investigation at the taxpayers’ expense,” an attorney for Slotkin said in a letter to Blanche this week. Slotkin is also one of the members of Congress the Justice Department failed to indict over the video. “There is no clearer telltale sign of a disassembling authoritarian leader than when he tries to prosecute those who simply speak up against him,” Slotkin said Thursday on X in response to Trump revisiting the video. “It’s also a desperate move to distract from the generational loss he’s brought to his party.” “So I say to President Trump and his Attorney General: Bring it. It would demonstrate to the country just how you’re hitting rock bottom,” she added. “And if that lets us then begin to recover and repair from your disastrous leadership, please just get on with it.”

articles.title: A 'really complicated job': Why midterm votes counting is taking so long in America's largest state
articles.summary: Alaskans are still waiting for the full results, including in the close Senate race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.
articles.body:
For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: midterm election ballots.

The regional airline is a piece of a complex logistical puzzle that sees Alaskans' ballots cast by mail and in person carried across the vast expanse of America's largest state, which is primarily connected by water and air rather than roads.

This considerable task explains why, a week after most US states knew their results in the midterms - in which the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress from the Republicans - Alaskans are still waiting for the Senate race to be called.

The victor in this close contest between the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former Congresswoman Mary Peltola, could remain unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots.

"We do feel a sense of pride of making sure we do the job right - the really complicated job of getting all these ballots across thousands of miles in Alaska," Andy Kline, the marketing director of Alaska Seaplanes, which serves the southeastern part of the state, told the BBC.

"We feel like we're part of the last leg of that journey of those ballots."

Some precincts in Alaska are able to communicate their initial results to centralised election offices on election night, allowing state officials and news outlets to report some preliminary vote tallies.

But it takes some time for the full picture of how people have voted to emerge.

As well as having the logistical challenge of counting votes from across a state more than six times the size of the UK, there is also a delay waiting for mail ballots to arrive, says Charles Stewart III, an election expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

These ballots can arrive up to 10 days later, or 15 days for overseas voters, if postmarked by election day.

Stewart said that election officials had "chosen to err on the side of getting it right rather than a rush to report the second and third tranches of ballots that get counted".

Regardless of whether ballots were cast in person or by mail, all of them eventually wind up in the state capital of Juneau – which is only reachable by plane or boat – for scanning and counting.

While more urban districts can get their materials on a plane late on election night, it takes longer for smaller or more remote parts of Alaska.

In some places, "you get someone who's basically running the election for their family and their neighbours because it's such a small village", says Scott Kendall, an election lawyer who previously worked on two campaigns for Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski.

In these smaller areas, ballots are sealed up in special envelopes or containers and sent it through the mail - which is where companies like Alaska Seaplanes comes in.

Ballots are put on the planes and sent to Juneau, where they then get dropped at the post office and delivered.

"It's part of our daily routine, just another couple of boxes," Kline said.

Once all the in-person and absentee mail ballots reach Juneau, election officials will complete their review.

If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote in the first round, officials will quickly use ranked-choice voting to re-allocate votes from the lowest-scoring candidates to their voters' second choices.

Then Alaska will finally declare a winner for its Senate race, as well as contests for governor and US House of Representatives.

Adding to the suspense of who will win the Senate race is the question of whether another Republican candidate called Dan Sullivan, who was allegedly recruited by Democratic operatives , would affect the outcome. Results released so far suggest a low probability.

This week, President Donald Trump alleged Alaska's Senate election had been "rigged" due to the second Dan's involvement. His administration is appealing its failed lawsuit to halt certification of the election over the issue, which a lower court dismissed.

Meanwhile, a judge has denied an attempt by Peltola's campaign to get information about how many absentee ballots election officials rejected, as well as information about those voters.

The state argued it had no obligation to share this data, and doing so would violate voter privacy.

While the result of the election is of the greatest importance to many, for people like Kline the process is also key.

"We're all citizens," he said of himself and his colleagues.

"We all feel like we have skin in the game to make sure that our elections are accurate and timely."

articles.body:
President Trump called outgoing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and told him to fight for his job ahead of his resignation, The New York Times reported on Thursday, citing two people briefed on the conversation.

Huang resigned as CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies after reports emerged of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a spy for the Chinese government.

The news shocked many in politics and tech, with Huang being a close ally of Trump’s amid the AI boom.

Trump said in an interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith on Thursday that he had called Huang on Wednesday, calling the situation “sad.”

“I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell,” Trump said. “What he feels most badly about is his wife and family … that’s what he told me.”

When asked if he thought Huang should have stepped down, Trump said it depends on if the woman he had an affair with was indeed a spy for China.

“The big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” Trump told Smith. “If the woman was a spy, yes.”

The markets soured following Huang’s departure and scandals, with Nvidia dipping more than 13 percent over the past five days.

Huang and Trump have maintained a close relationship as the AI boom has dramatically increased the need for Nvidia’s high-powered chips. At the end of last year, Trump reversed course and allowed Nvidia to sell its H200 chips to China, a big win for the company.

Now, Huang’s relationship with a possible Chinese spy is raising national security concerns.

Members of both parties have called for Congress to look into Huang’s relationship and to pass restrictions on Chinese access to advanced chips. Democrats are already calling for investigations into what Trump knew about the matter.

The Times previously reported Trump was told multiple times that Huang was close to the suspected spy, but he apparently did not take action and still allowed the chips to be sold to China.
